tricks.reason: Two independent reputable Logic sources describe exactly this: after making a marquee selection, a single click inside it with the Pointer splits the regions at both marquee boundaries. One caveat worth adding to the body copy for safety — the sources note you should click on the top region of a multi-track marquee, otherwise the whole selection is dragged/moved to the click position instead of being split in place.
tricks.evidence_quote: Once a Marquee area has been created, clicking within it with many of the other tools causes all the regions within the Marquee area to be split at the Marquee-area boundaries... to split the regions within the Marquee area without moving them, be sure to click on the top region; otherwise the whole selection will be moved to the click location.

tricks.title: Set the locators to the marquee instantly
tricks.reason: The key command is wrong. Every external source that documents setting the locators from a marquee selection gives ⌘U, not plain U — and ⌘U is the command that ALSO enables Cycle, which makes the trick's "then C" step unnecessary. studio-interns.com's key-command entry is titled "Set Locators/Loop by Regions/Events/Marquee and Enable Cycle/Loop ⌘U"; a second Logic tutorial source says after a marquee selection "you can press CMD + U, and you will set the left and right cycle locators to your selection". One shortcut cheat-sheet aggregation additionally reports plain U as "Set Rounded Locators by Regions/Events", i.e. a different command. As written ("hitting U sets the cycle locators to exactly that range... Marquee then U then C") the trick would leave a buyer pressing a key that does something else, or nothing.
tricks.evidence_quote: Set Locators/Loop by Regions/Events/Marquee and Enable Cycle/Loop ⌘U
tricks.correction: With a marquee selection active, press ⌘U — Set Locators/Loop by Regions/Events/Marquee and Enable Cycle/Loop. It snaps the cycle locators to exactly that range and switches Cycle on in the same keystroke, so marquee then ⌘U gives you a perfect loop in two moves, not three. (Cycle can still be toggled on and off afterwards with C.)

tricks.title: Marquee automation to move only that range
tricks.reason: Apple's automation-points page describes precisely this behaviour: a marquee selection spanning automation data auto-creates points at both edges when you edit it, which is what lets you raise or lower only that section without affecting what is on either side. Apple specifies two points at each edge (so the flanking values are held), which the body copy could state, but nothing here is contradicted.
tricks.evidence_quote: When you edit automation data that is spanned by a marquee selection, two automation points are automatically created at the left edge, and two at the right edge, of the selection.

tricks.title: Use marquee to create a drop
tricks.reason: This is workflow advice, but it rests on a checkable claim — that a marquee across every track plus Delete produces arrangement-wide silence for that time range in one action — and that claim is documented. Apple states a marquee-ruler drag selects across all tracks and that deleting is one of the edits available on the selected area; a second Logic source confirms the Delete/Backspace keystroke makes the selected area disappear.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can drag in the marquee ruler to create a marquee selection across all tracks... You can perform most edits, such as moving, cutting, copying, and deleting, in the selected area.

tricks.title: ⌥‑drag a marquee selection to copy that time range
tricks.reason: Two independent reputable Logic sources describe Option-dragging a marquee selection as a copy that leaves the source region intact — Sound On Sound explicitly notes the cuts in the original marquee area are healed afterwards, which is the trick's "without disturbing the surrounding regions". Marquee selection is documented by Apple as working on parts of regions generally, so the audio-and-MIDI framing is not contradicted, though no source I found tests MIDI specifically.
tricks.evidence_quote: Option-drag with the Pointer tool to copy the highlighted area to another place in the timeline, and the cuts in the original marquee selection are automatically 'healed' and will no longer be visible.

tricks.title: Marquee inside a take folder to edit, not to comp
tricks.reason: Both claims check out. Apple/Logic Studio Training document the two take-folder modes: with Quick Swipe Comping on you swipe to choose the best parts of takes; switching it off enables the cutting and editing tools, the Marquee among them, so the tool becomes a region-editing tool inside the folder rather than a comping tool.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can deactivate Quick Swipe Comping and enable cutting and editing tools (such as the Scissors and Marquee tools) by pressing the Quick Swipe Comping button.

tricks.title: Hold ⇧ to extend an existing marquee
tricks.reason: Apple's guide documents Shift-clicking to change an existing marquee selection edge by edge, which is exactly the trick's claim and its k field. Apple adds a useful refinement the body copy could mention: Shift-click moves the selection end nearest the pointer, Option-Shift-click moves the far end.
tricks.evidence_quote: Press and hold Shift, then click in the Tracks area to change the selection in any direction... Shift-click inside a selection to move the selection end closest to the pointer. Option-Shift-click inside a selection to move the selection end farther from the pointer.

downgrades.title: Click any region after marqueeing to split at the marquee edges
downgrades.reason: The auditor's own cited source contradicts the trick's title, and the auditor noticed this yet still cleared it as VERIFIED. I re-ran the search and confirmed the Sound On Sound sentence verbatim: 'to split the regions within the Marquee area without moving them, be sure to click on the top region; otherwise the whole selection will be moved to the click location.' The trick says 'Click ANY region' and the body says 'single-click inside it, and Logic splits the regions at both marquee boundaries automatically.' Per the only evidence on offer, clicking any region other than the top one does NOT split - it DRAGS the entire multi-track selection to wherever the reader clicked. That is a destructive misfire on a trick badged 'GAME CHANGER': a buyer following it literally on a multi-track marquee will move their audio, not cut it, and will reasonably call the book inaccurate. Secondary problem: the source is an undated Sound On Sound Logic column with no version label, so even the corrected behaviour is not confirmed for 10.7/11/12 specifically. CORRECTION (externally sourced, soundonsound.com/techniques/marquee-tool-tips-logic): retitle to 'Click the TOP region after marqueeing to split at the marquee edges' and add to the body: 'On a marquee spanning several tracks, click the topmost region in the selection - clicking a lower one moves the whole selection to the click position instead of splitting it.' With that caveat in the body copy the trick is sound; as written it is not.

downgrades.title: Marquee inside a take folder to edit, not to comp
downgrades.reason: The evidence_quote is reconstructed, not real page text. The auditor quotes logicstudiotraining.com as saying 'You can deactivate Quick Swipe Comping and enable cutting and editing tools (such as the Scissors and Marquee tools) by pressing the Quick Swipe Comping button.' I searched that exact page. What it actually describes is toggling via 'the down pointing triangle in the upper right corner of the Take Folder' or the key command Option-Q, and it names the SCISSORS tool - 'Quick Swipe Comping mode must not be active to utilize the capability of cutting take folders with the Scissors tool.' The Marquee, which is the entire claim under test, was not confirmed anywhere in the returned text, and the 'Quick Swipe Comping button' mechanism does not match the page's own description. The quote reads as memory dressed as a citation. Three further failures: (1) the source is a single wiki, not the two independent reputable sources the rules require, and a wiki is the weakest tier; (2) 'Logic Studio' was Apple's Logic 8/9-era bundle (2007-2011), so this is a pre-Logic-Pro-X page being used to verify a claim about 10.7/11/12 - the exact version trap flagged in the brief; (3) the auditor's reason says 'Apple/Logic Studio Training document the two take-folder modes' but no Apple URL was ever cited. The trick also asserts unverified specifics of its own: 'Comping is swiping with the Pointer while Quick Swipe Comping is on' names a tool no cited source names. SALVAGE - keep the toggle, drop the tool list: 'A take folder has two modes. With Quick Swipe Comping on, dragging across takes builds a comp. Switch it off from the menu in the take folder's top-right corner, and the folder stops behaving like a comping surface and starts behaving like a region you can cut and edit. If your edits inside a take folder keep turning into comp swipes, this toggle is why.' That version asserts only the mode toggle and drops the unproven claim that the Marquee specifically becomes available.

downgrades.title: ⌥‑drag a marquee selection to copy that time range
downgrades.reason: The auditor's own reason concedes the case: 'no source I found tests MIDI specifically' - yet the body copy states the trick 'Copies the audio AND MIDI inside the marquee', and it was still cleared VERIFIED. A verdict of VERIFIED requires the source to support the claim exactly as written; half the claim is admittedly unsupported. Additional defects: (1) the reason claims 'Two independent reputable Logic sources' but only one URL and one quote were supplied, and the second was never named - a bare assertion of corroboration is not corroboration; (2) I confirmed the Sound On Sound 'healed' sentence is real at soundonsound.com/techniques/marque-distinction, but I could not establish a publication year for it, and its punning Logic-column style points to a pre-10.7 era, so it is not version-matched to 10.7/11/12; (3) the body promises the copy lands 'without disturbing the surrounding regions', while the quoted source only supports the SOURCE area being healed - it says nothing about what happens to existing regions at the DESTINATION, where a dropped copy will overlap whatever is already there. SALVAGE - keep the sourced half, drop the MIDI claim and the destination over-promise: 'Hold Option and drag a marquee selection with the Pointer to copy that slice of audio elsewhere in the timeline. The cuts left behind in the original marquee area heal automatically, so the source material is left as you found it. Check what is already sitting at the destination before you drop, and audition the result.' That keeps the useful move and asserts only what the source states.

audit.search_note: WebSearch worked throughout; support.apple.com is egress-blocked for WebFetch, so all Apple evidence comes from search snippets that quote the guide pages directly. 21 searches used, covering: Show Automation/A key, track vs region automation, Mix > Convert Automation, automation modes (Read/Touch/Latch/Write/Trim/Relative), Mix > Delete Automation, Automation settings pane, Select/copy/move automation, Control-Shift curve drag, marquee boundary points, Command-click tool assignment, Snap Automation, Pencil tool, automation lanes disclosure triangle, plug-in bypass automation, Delete Redundant Automation Points. Genuinely unresolved after searching (marked UNVERIFIABLE, not skipped): (a) whether ⌘-drag is the *default* marquee shortcut — Apple documents the Command-click tool as user-assignable and the tool menus only appear with Complete Features enabled, and a Logic Pro Help thread exists titled "Why am I not getting the marquee tool as a shortcut when I hit Command?"; (b) whether Mix > Show Automation or a disclosure arrow reveals *every* automated parameter (the disclosure-triangle/Option-click behaviour is documented only in the Logic Pro 9 manual and secondary sites, and it is at the lower-left of the track header, not "the bottom of an open automation lane"); (c) whether plug-in bypass is automatable for *every* plug-in (forum-level evidence only, plus reports of slot-specific and 11.2 version bugs); (d) whether a whole-project "delete all automation" command exists — Apple's Delete automation page lists only the three "…on Selected Track" variants in every snippet returned. One further caveat not counted as a verdict: Apple's Delete automation page never lists "Delete Redundant Automation Points" under Mix > Delete Automation; the command's existence is confirmed only as a key command (⌃⌫) via studio-interns.com, so the menu path in that trick may also be wrong.

tricks.title: Know the difference between Track and Region automation
tricks.reason: Apple confirms the A key opens automation view and confirms both mechanisms exactly as described (track automation stays fixed to the timeline, region automation travels with the region). Caveat worth a copy tweak: Apple's wording for the switch is the automation controls in the track header; the Apple page does not literally say "dropdown", that wording is supported only by secondary sources (skydocu mirror of Logic Pro Help, dummies.com).
tricks.evidence_quote: With track automation, if you re-record, move, or copy regions (either to another point on the same track or to another track entirely) the automation data remains tied to the initial point on the track in which it was created. However, with region automation … if you move or copy the region (either to another point on the same track, or to another track) the automation remains with the region. [and, from the Show automation curves page:] choose Mix > Show Automation (or press A)

tricks.title: Use Region automation for anything that belongs to the part
tricks.reason: Apple's track-vs-region page states exactly this behavioural difference, and specifically recommends region automation for instrument parameters — which is what a filter sweep inside a synth riff is.
tricks.evidence_quote: with region automation … if you move or copy the region (either to another point on the same track, or to another track) the automation remains with the region. Region automation is particularly useful when you are automating instrument parameters.

tricks.title: Convert between the two without redrawing
tricks.reason: The menu path and the exact command name are confirmed, and the reverse command exists too (four commands total: Convert Visible/All Track Automation to Region Automation, and Convert Visible/All Region Automation to Track Automation). FLAG for the owner: the trailing sentence "Nothing is lost either way" is not stated by any source found and is the one clause a buyer could argue with — recommend softening it to "the curves are carried over rather than redrawn".
tricks.evidence_quote: "Convert Visible Track Automation to Region Automation" is a command found in the Mix > Convert Automation submenu that converts displayed track automation to region automation … "Convert Visible Region Automation to Track Automation" … "Convert All Track Automation to Region Automation" … "Convert All Region Automation to Track Automation"

tricks.title: Press A to toggle automation view
tricks.reason: Apple's Show automation curves page gives the A key command explicitly alongside the menu route, for the 10.7 guide and the current (11.x/12) guide alike.
tricks.evidence_quote: To show automation in Logic Pro, you can choose Mix > Show Automation (or press A).

tricks.title: Use Latch mode for almost everything
tricks.reason: All four mode descriptions match Apple's own definitions: Latch holds the new value after release, Touch returns to existing automation, Write erases, Read plays back only. "Latch is the right default" is opinion and not a checkable claim.
tricks.evidence_quote: Read: Plays back all automation that exists on the track … You can't change the value … Touch: … After the fader or knob is released, the parameter follows existing automation on the track. Latch: Works like Touch mode, but after the fader or knob is released, the new parameter value replaces existing automation on the track.

tricks.title: Never leave a track in Write mode
tricks.reason: Apple documents exactly the destructive behaviour claimed, including erasure when you touch nothing at all. The "destroyed more mixes than any other setting" line is rhetoric, not a checkable claim.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Write mode, existing track automation data is erased as the playhead passes it. If you move any of the Mixer's controls, this movement is recorded; if you don't, existing data is simply deleted as the playhead passes it.

tricks.title: Draw automation with the Pencil tool for precision
tricks.reason: Apple documents the Pencil tool as the tool for drawing series of automation points (with curved/stepped variants governed by the Automation settings). The comparative claim ("faster and more accurate than performing it") is taste, and the mechanism it rests on is confirmed.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can use the Pencil Tool to draw multiple automation points on an automation curve. With Logic Pro in automation mode, click-drag or Option-click-drag the Pencil Tool across the automation curve.

tricks.title: Delete an automation point without dragging it
tricks.reason: All three methods named in the trick appear verbatim in Apple's Delete automation page: double-click, select then Delete, and the Eraser tool.
tricks.evidence_quote: With Logic Pro in automation mode, you can double-click the automation point, select the automation point then press Delete, or drag across the automation point with the Eraser tool.

tricks.title: Curve any line by dragging its middle with ⌃⇧
tricks.reason: The modifier in the k field matches Apple exactly (Control-Shift drag with the Pointer tool on the curve between two points), and it holds for the 10.7 and current guides.
tricks.evidence_quote: Hold down Control-Shift while dragging an automation curve with the Pointer tool. An automation curve between two automation points represents continuously changing parameter values.

tricks.title: Trim automation up or down as a group
tricks.reason: Two problems against Apple's own text. (1) There is no standalone "Trim mode" to sit in — Apple states Trim "works in combination with Touch and Latch automation modes", so the reader following this will look for a mode that does nothing on its own. (2) Apple restricts Trim to Volume, Pan and Send levels, and describes it as offsetting by the amount you move the control as you pass over the automation — not as shifting "the entire existing automation curve" in one gesture, which is what the 1 dB vocal example implies.
tricks.evidence_quote: Trim: Offsets the value of the existing automation (Volume, Pan, Send levels) by adjusting it up or down by the amount you move the fader or control. Works in combination with Touch and Latch automation modes.
tricks.correction: Trim is not a mode on its own — you switch it on in combination with Touch or Latch. Once it is on, moving the fader offsets the existing automation up or down by the amount you move, keeping the shape of the curve, and it applies to Volume, Pan and Send levels. Run the section you want to lift with Trim Latch engaged to push a whole automated vocal up by a decibel.

tricks.title: Use Relative mode to layer a second pass
tricks.reason: Apple describes Relative exactly as an added secondary curve that offsets the existing primary curve, i.e. the original moves survive. Worth knowing (not contradicted by the trick): Apple scopes it to Volume, Pan and Send levels, and it combines with Touch, Latch and Write.
tricks.evidence_quote: Relative: Adds a secondary automation curve that offsets the existing primary curve for the selected parameter (Volume, Pan, Send levels). Works in combination with Touch, Latch, and Write automation modes.

tricks.title: Marquee a range then drag the line to change only that section
tricks.reason: The body copy is confirmed — Apple states that editing automation spanned by a marquee selection auto-creates points at both edges, so the change cannot bleed outwards. What I could NOT confirm is the k field, "⌘ + drag": Apple documents the Command-click tool as something you assign yourself ("click the Command-click Tool menu, then choose a tool"), the Command-click/Right-click Tool menus only appear when Complete Features is enabled in Preferences > Advanced, and a Logic Pro Help thread exists titled "Why am I not getting the marquee tool as a shortcut when I hit Command?". No source found says Marquee is the factory default for Command-click, so the shortcut as printed will fail for some buyers.
tricks.evidence_quote: When you edit automation data that is spanned by a marquee selection, two automation points are automatically created at the left edge, and two at the right edge, of the selection.
tricks.salvage: Select the Marquee tool and drag across the bars you want to change, then drag the automation line inside that selection. Logic creates two automation points at each edge of the marquee automatically, so the change is boxed in and does not bleed into the surrounding bars. If you have assigned Marquee as your Command-click tool (Logic Pro > Preferences > Advanced must have the full feature set enabled for that menu to appear), you can hold Command to grab it without switching tools.

tricks.title: Show every automated parameter at once
tricks.reason: Two unsupported specifics. Apple documents Mix > Show Automation only as showing automation curves (the same thing A does) — nothing found says it reveals every parameter containing data. And the disclosure control that opens extra lanes is at the lower left of the track header, not "at the bottom of an open automation lane"; a single click opens one further lane, and it is Option-click that opens many lanes for already-recorded parameters. That behaviour is documented in the Logic Pro 9 manual and repeated on dummies.com and LogicProGEM, but I found no current-guide (10.7/11/12) Apple confirmation, so the version status is unproven.
tricks.evidence_quote: To display additional automation lanes, click the disclosure triangle to the lower left of a track name, which opens a separate automation sub-lane, below the track … Option-click the (closed) triangle to open up to 30 automation subtracks, which will display existing (already recorded) automation data.
tricks.salvage: Press A to show automation, then click the small disclosure triangle at the lower left of the track header to open an extra automation lane underneath the track. Repeat it to stack more lanes, and pick the parameter for each lane from the automation parameter pop-up menu in its header — that way you can see several written parameters side by side instead of flipping between them.

tricks.title: Copy automation between tracks
tricks.reason: Apple's procedure explicitly has you move the playhead to the insertion point first, and states the paste lands at the playhead position — not at the same timeline position it was copied from. A buyer following the trick as written will get the automation dropped wherever the playhead happens to be.
tricks.evidence_quote: Drag across the region with the Marquee tool. Choose Edit > Copy from the Tracks area menu bar. Select the track you want to copy the automation data to, then move the playhead to the insertion point. Choose Edit > Paste from the Tracks area menu bar. The region selection, along with its automation, is copied to the target track at the playhead position.
tricks.correction: Drag across the range with the Marquee tool and choose Edit > Copy. Select the destination track, move the playhead to the point where you want the data to start, then choose Edit > Paste — the automation lands at the playhead, so park the playhead deliberately (or set it from the original selection first) if you want the copy to sit at the same bar.

tricks.title: Delete all automation on a track in one command
tricks.reason: The named command is confirmed verbatim — Mix > Delete Automation > Delete All Automation on Selected Track. But the second sentence is not: every snippet of Apple's Delete automation page lists only three commands, all scoped to the selected track (Delete Visible / Delete All / Delete Orphaned Automation on Selected Track). No whole-project equivalent turned up in the current guide, so "Also available for the whole project" is an unsupported claim a buyer can check in ten seconds.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Logic Pro, you can choose options from Mix > Delete Automation: Delete Visible Automation on Selected Track removes automation for the active automation parameter; Delete All Automation on Selected Track removes all automation from the selected track; and Delete Orphaned Automation on Selected Track removes all orphaned automation from the selected track.
tricks.salvage: Mix > Delete Automation > Delete All Automation on Selected Track wipes every parameter on that track in one move. The same submenu also holds Delete Visible Automation on Selected Track, which clears only the parameter currently displayed, and Delete Orphaned Automation on Selected Track for data left behind by plug-ins you have removed.

tricks.title: Automation follows regions if you tell it to
tricks.reason: The setting name, its location in the Automation settings pane, and all three pop-up values (Never / Always / Ask) are confirmed, as is the described behaviour of dragging a region taking its automation along.
tricks.evidence_quote: The "Move Track Automation with Regions" pop-up menu determines what happens to automation data when you move regions … Never: Doesn't move automation when you move regions. Always: Always moves automation when you move regions. Ask: A dialog prompts you to move the automation data—or leave it where it is—whenever you move a region.

tricks.title: Thin dense automation after recording a controller pass
tricks.reason: The command exists, but not as the trick describes it. Delete Redundant Automation Points is global — it removes redundant points on all regions and all tracks — so "Select the range, then …" is misleading: the selection does not scope it, and a reader will unknowingly rewrite automation across the whole project. Separately, Apple's Delete automation page does not list this command under Mix > Delete Automation at all (it lists only the three Selected Track commands); the command is documented as a key command, ⌃⌫.
tricks.evidence_quote: Delete Redundant Automation Points ⌃⌫ … removes all redundant automation points on all regions and tracks.
tricks.correction: Recording modwheel or a fader creates thousands of points. Delete Redundant Automation Points (key command Control-Delete) strips the points that do not change the shape of the curve — but note it is a global command: it acts on all regions and all tracks, not just the range you have selected. To thin one passage only, select the points in that range with the Marquee or Pointer tool and press Delete, then redraw.

tricks.title: Snap automation to the grid when it needs to be rhythmic
tricks.reason: Automation does not simply obey the same Snap setting as regions. Apple documents a separate Snap Automation submenu inside the Snap pop-up with its own value, set independently in the Tracks area and the Piano Roll Editor. A reader who sets the region Snap value expecting automation to follow will not get the behaviour promised.
tricks.evidence_quote: choose Snap Automation from the Snap pop-up menu and select a value from the submenu, after which automation edits snap to the value chosen in the Snap Automation submenu … it can be set independently in the Tracks area and the Piano Roll Editor
tricks.correction: Automation snaps to its own grid value, set separately from regions: open the Snap pop-up menu in the Tracks area, choose Snap Automation, and pick a value from the submenu. Automation edits then snap to that value, and you can set it independently in the Tracks area and the Piano Roll Editor — so your filter stabs land on the beat without changing how regions snap.

tricks.title: Automate plugin bypass for effect changes
tricks.reason: No Apple guide page found that states plug-in bypass is an automatable parameter, let alone that it is available for every plug-in. Support for the practice is forum-level only (Logic Pro Help, Logic Users Group), and the same searches surfaced counter-reports — a Gearspace thread "Can't automate plugin bypass on 6th plugin slot" and an Apple Community thread about bypass automation breaking in Logic Pro 11.2 (reportedly fixed in 11.2.1). The universal "Every plugin's bypass state is automatable" is exactly the kind of absolute a buyer can disprove with one plug-in.
tricks.evidence_quote: select the lane for "insert bypass," which is one of the parameters for an effect and works the same way as any other parameter
tricks.salvage: Insert bypass usually appears in the track's automation parameter pop-up menu alongside the plug-in's own parameters, so you can switch an effect in and out on the timeline. Automating a delay in and out this way is cleaner than riding its mix knob. Check the parameter list for the slot in question before you commit to the approach — bypass is not exposed identically for every plug-in and every insert slot.

tricks.title: Automate send levels rather than plugin mix knobs
tricks.reason: Pure workflow preference. The only underlying assertions — that a send has a fader on the mixer and its own automation lane — are generic and not the sort of specific, checkable claim a buyer would dispute. Nothing here asserts a menu path, key command, version or mechanism.

downgrades.title: Know the difference between Track and Region automation
downgrades.reason: The auditor cleared this while admitting in its own reason that Apple never says "dropdown" — that admission should have been the verdict. Apple's "Show automation curves in Logic Pro" page (https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/show-automation-curves-lgcpb1a3f099/10.7/mac/11.0) enumerates the track header controls as three separate things: "An Automation button, an Automation Parameter pop-up menu, and an Automation Mode pop-up menu appear in each track header," and assigns the Track/Region switch to the button, not a menu: "You can click the Automation button in the track header to switch between track automation and region automation." I got that same sentence back from two independently phrased searches of that page. So the track header does contain two dropdowns — Automation Parameter and Automation Mode — and NEITHER of them switches Track/Region. A reader following the book opens a pop-up menu, finds Volume/Pan/plug-in parameters or Read/Touch/Latch/Write, and never finds the Track/Region choice the book promised. That is a buyer-visible dead end, not a wording quibble. Secondary flaw: the auditor's evidence_quote splices two different Apple pages into one quotation and attributes both to the track-vs-region URL, which does not contain the "press A" line at all. SOURCED CORRECTION (Apple, Show automation curves): "Press A to show automation, then click the Automation button in the track header to switch between Track automation (fixed to the timeline) and Region automation (travels with the region when you move it). Choosing wrong is why your automation ends up in the wrong place." The A key and both behavioural descriptions are verified; only the control name needs replacing.

downgrades.title: Convert between the two without redrawing
downgrades.reason: The auditor wrote that the closing sentence "Nothing is lost either way" is "not stated by any source found and is the one clause a buyer could argue with" — and then stamped the trick VERIFIED anyway. Under the standing rule (source must support the claim AS WRITTEN), an unsourced absolute about data integrity cannot ride along inside a VERIFIED trick; it is the single most refund-triggering sentence in the group. I confirmed the rest: the command name and the Mix > Convert Automation submenu path check out (search of "Convert Visible Track Automation to Region Automation" returns Apple's track-vs-region page plus the statement that the command "can be found in the Mix > Convert Automation submenu"). What no source supports is losslessness in both directions, and there is positive reason for doubt rather than confidence: Apple's own automation-boundary language elsewhere ("The automation data area encompassed by the region boundaries is moved," plus the separate "Include trails, if possible" checkbox that exists precisely because automation lying outside a region's boundaries is handled differently) shows Logic treats region boundaries as a real limit on what automation a region can carry. Track automation sitting where no region exists has nowhere to go in a track-to-region conversion. Unproven either way, so it must not be asserted. SALVAGE (drop the last sentence, keep the verified path): "Mix > Convert Automation > Convert Visible Track Automation to Region Automation, and the reverse, Convert Visible Region Automation to Track Automation. There are 'All' variants of both commands. The curves are carried over rather than redrawn — check the result at region edges before you delete anything."

downgrades.title: Automation follows regions if you tell it to
downgrades.reason: The setting name, the three pop-up values and the behaviour are all fine — Apple confirms "The 'Move Track Automation with Regions' pop-up menu determines what happens to automation data when you move regions … Never: Doesn't move automation when you move regions. Always: Always moves automation when you move regions. The automation data area encompassed by the region boundaries is moved. Ask: A dialog prompts you to move the automation data—or leave it where it is—whenever you move a region." The failure is the menu path, which the auditor waved through as "location in the Automation settings pane confirmed." It is not confirmed as written. Both of my searches — including one that returned Apple's current https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/automation-settings-lgcp8aa8f24b/mac page as the top hit — reported the access route as "Logic Pro > Preferences > Automation (or using the Open Automation Preferences key command)," and the Logic Pro X help mirror and Apple's older help pages title the pane "Automation preferences." This is the version trap in its usual form: the book covers 10.7, 11 and 12, and "Settings" is the post-Ventura name only. In Logic Pro 10.7 the reader must go to Logic Pro > Preferences > Automation; there is no Settings item in that menu. A 10.7 buyer follows the path and hits nothing. The trick states one path and does not scope it. SOURCED CORRECTION: "Open the Automation pane of Logic's settings — Logic Pro > Settings > Automation in Logic Pro 11 and 12, Logic Pro > Preferences > Automation in 10.7 — and set the 'Move Track Automation with Regions' pop-up to Always, or Ask if you want the choice each time. With Always, the automation inside the region's boundaries travels when you drag the region." Worth adding for accuracy, also from Apple's page: the neighbouring 'Include trails, if possible' checkbox decides whether automation in the empty space after a region comes along too.

audit.search_note: WebSearch worked normally; 15 of the ~20 budgeted calls used. Searches were aimed at whole Apple User Guide pages (Pattern creation basics, Step Sequencer overview, Use edit modes, Edit rows, Step Sequencer inspector, Modify pattern playback, Load and save patterns, Convert region pages, Step Sequencer key commands / pointer shortcuts) rather than per-claim, which settled most of the section. Two items could not be nailed down and are called out in their reasons: (a) the exact list of Step Rate note values — I could NOT confirm that "1/12" appears in Logic's Step Rate menu, only that triplet values exist, so nothing in this report certifies "1/12"; (b) an Option-click-to-reset shortcut for steps, which does not appear on Apple's "Edit Step Sequencer steps" or "Pointer shortcuts for Step Sequencer" pages. The "E" key command is supported only by secondary Logic-education sites (two independent ones agreeing), not by a quotable Apple page — treated as verified under the two-source rule but flagged. This file has no group-level "path" fields, so there were no menu paths to check.

tricks.title: Create a Pattern Region to open the Step Sequencer
tricks.reason: Apple's 'Pattern creation basics' page documents exactly this route (Control-click = right-click) on a software instrument track, which covers the book's 'drum or instrument track'. The 'E' half of the trick is supported only by secondary Logic-education sources that agree with each other, not by a quotable Apple page; it is not contradicted anywhere. Minor caveat the owner may want to note: Apple does not explicitly state that creating the pattern region auto-opens the Step Sequencer in the Editors area — it also documents 'select an empty MIDI region, click the Step Sequencer button in the Editors area'.
tricks.evidence_quote: Control-click in an empty software instrument track, then choose Create Pattern Region from the shortcut menu. Alternatively, you can select an empty MIDI region, click the Step Sequencer button in the Editors area, then click a step in the step grid.

tricks.title: Give every row a different step rate
tricks.reason: The underlying capability is real — Apple confirms per-row step rate — but the UI control named in the trick is not. Apple's enumeration of what is in a Step Sequencer row header is 'a row icon, a disclosure arrow to show subrows, and a set of controls for the row, including Mute and Solo buttons, a Row Assignment pop-up menu, Rotate buttons, and Increment/Decrement controls' — there is no 'edit button'. The documented routes are the Row inspector's Step Rate pop-up menu ('To change the step rate for the row, you choose a note value for steps in the row from the Step Rate pop-up menu', reached by clicking a row header then clicking Row in the Step Sequencer inspector) and the Step Rate edit mode ('Drag vertically in the step to set the length of the step'). Separately, I could not confirm that '1/12' is an available Step Rate value — only that triplet values exist — so the correction below drops it rather than repeating an unsourced option name.
tricks.evidence_quote: Each row header contains a row icon, a disclosure arrow to show subrows, and a set of controls for the row, including Mute and Solo buttons, a Row Assignment pop-up menu, Rotate buttons, and Increment/Decrement controls. […] To change the step rate for the row, you choose a note value for steps in the row from the Step Rate pop-up menu.
tricks.correction: Rows do not have to share the pattern's subdivision. Click a row header to select the row, then in the Step Sequencer inspector click Row and choose a note value from the Step Rate pop-up menu. (You can also switch the grid to Step Rate edit mode and drag vertically inside a single step to change just that step.) Hi-hats at 1/16 against a kick at 1/8 gives you cross-rhythms with no extra work at all.

tricks.title: Set different pattern lengths per row
tricks.reason: Apple confirms per-row length is a real setting, which is the only factual claim here. The arithmetic checks out independently: a 16-step row against a 15-step row realigns at the least common multiple, 240 steps.
tricks.evidence_quote: each row can have its own length, step rate, playback mode, start offset, and other settings

tricks.title: Use the row's Playback Mode for variation
tricks.reason: All seven mode names in the trick match Apple's Playback Mode pop-up menu exactly, and the menu is per-row as the trick states. Random is described as completely random and nonlooping, which supports 'the pattern changes every bar on its own'.
tricks.evidence_quote: Forward: Steps play from left to right. Backward: Steps play from right to left. Ping-Pong: Playback alternates between left to right and right to left. Pendulum: Similar to Ping-Pong, but the first and last steps aren't repeated. Wander: Playback randomly alternates between left to right and right to left. Shuffle: The playback order of all steps is shuffled for each loop. Random: The playback order of steps is completely random and nonlooping.

tricks.title: Increase pattern length beyond 16 steps
tricks.reason: 64 steps is confirmed as the pattern-length maximum, and Apple documents changing it from the Pattern Length pop-up menu in the Step Sequencer menu bar. Nothing version-specific here — the ceiling has been 64 since Step Sequencer shipped in 10.5, so it holds across 10.7/11/12.
tricks.evidence_quote: Patterns can be from 12 to 64 steps in length, allowing for different time signatures and multiple bar patterns.

tricks.title: Switch the edit mode to change what you are drawing
tricks.reason: Every mode named in the trick appears on Apple's edit modes page, and the page confirms the 'and more' (Step Rate, Note, Octave, Start Offset, On/Off). One naming nit worth a copy-edit: Apple calls the mode 'Loop Start/End', not 'Loop Start' — a reader will still find it in the menu, and the book's own later trick uses the full name.
tricks.evidence_quote: Skip: Click a step to turn skipping on or off. When skipping is on, the step is skipped and playback moves immediately to the next step. Loop Start/End: When this mode is active, a frame appears around the row… Velocity: Drag vertically in the step to set the Velocity value from 1 to 127

tricks.title: Use Chance to make a pattern breathe
tricks.reason: Apple confirms Chance is a per-step percentage probability that the step plays on each pattern repetition. The book's arithmetic (40% ≈ twice every five bars) follows from that as long as the pattern is one bar long, which is the default (16 steps at 1/16). Worth adding 'in a one-bar pattern' if the owner wants it airtight.
tricks.evidence_quote: Drag vertically in the step to set the Chance percentage. Chance controls the probability that the step plays each time the pattern repeats.

tricks.title: Use Note Repeat for rolls without drawing them
tricks.reason: Apple documents Note Repeat as a per-step value from 1 to 16 controlling how often the note repeats within the step's duration. Since 1 means the note sounds once, a value of 4 means it fires four times inside that step, exactly as written.
tricks.evidence_quote: Drag vertically in the step to set the Note Repeat value from 1 to 16. Note Repeat controls how often the note repeats during the duration of the step.

tricks.title: Set Gate to shorten or lengthen individual hits
tricks.reason: Apple states Gate only shortens: it sets the note length as a percentage of the step and shortens it to less than the step's duration. Gate cannot lengthen a note past its step, so 'or lengthen' is wrong, and 'long gates create glides' is wrong twice over — a full-length gate is just a full-length note, and joining notes across steps is what Tie does ('The duration of the step is lengthened by the value of the step it is tied to'). The 'per-step, not per-pattern' claim is correct and survives.
tricks.evidence_quote: Drag vertically in the step to set the Gate value as a percentage of the step. The Gate value shortens the note length to less than the duration of the step.
tricks.correction: Gate sets a step's note length as a percentage of the step, shortening it to less than the step's full duration — short gates on a bass pattern give you staccato stabs. It only ever shortens; to make a note run longer than its step, switch to Tie edit mode and click the right edge of the step to tie it to the following one, which lengthens its duration by the value of the step it is tied to. Both are per-step, not per-pattern.

tricks.title: Tie steps together for sustained notes
tricks.reason: Apple's Tie edit mode does exactly this — joining a step to the adjacent step so the duration extends across both, which is what makes sustained bass and lead writing possible in the grid.
tricks.evidence_quote: In the Tie edit mode, you can click the right edge of a step to tie it to the following step, or click the left edge to tie it to the previous step. The duration of the step is lengthened by the value of the step it is tied to.

tricks.title: ⌥‑click a step to reset it to default
tricks.reason: No external source found either way. Apple's 'Edit Step Sequencer steps' page and its dedicated 'Pointer shortcuts for Step Sequencer' page do not list any Option-click reset; the documented modifier on those pages is Option-Shift-drag, which creates a value ramp across steps, and the documented way to reset a step is Functions > Clear Step, which 'resets all their edit mode values to default values'. The claim that Option-click works 'on every parameter in every edit mode' is exactly the sort of plausible-sounding blanket assertion that needs a citation and does not have one. Note this is not a contradiction — Apple simply never documents it — so it is UNVERIFIABLE, not WRONG.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can clear steps, which resets all their edit mode values to default values (for the step rate, the default is defined by the row step rate). […] choose Functions > Clear Step from the Step Sequencer menu bar.
tricks.salvage: Reset a step you have over-edited: select the step, then choose Functions > Clear Step from the Step Sequencer menu bar. That clears all of the step's edit-mode values back to their defaults in one move — for step rate, the default is whatever the row's step rate is. (Retitle the trick 'Clear a step to reset all its edit-mode values' and drop the ⌥ + click key command field, which is not documented.)

tricks.title: Use the Step Sequencer on any software instrument
tricks.reason: Apple states outright that Step Sequencer works with any available software instrument for note-based as well as drum patterns, and separately documents switching a row to pitches via the Row Assignment menu (choose Notes and pick a note value, or Melodic to assign different pitches to different steps).
tricks.evidence_quote: Using Step Sequencer, you can create rhythm-based drum patterns and note-based instrument patterns using any available software instrument.

tricks.title: Automate plugin parameters per step
tricks.reason: Apple documents the Add Row pop-up menu above the row headers and confirms an automation row can be assigned to any automatable parameter, plug-in parameters explicitly included — which is precisely the filter-cutoff-per-step use the trick describes.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Step Sequencer, click the Add Row pop-up menu above the row headers… You can assign an automation row to any automatable parameter, including MIDI continuous controller (CC) parameters, channel strip controls, plug-in parameters, and Smart Controls.

tricks.title: Convert a pattern region to MIDI to edit it in the Piano Roll
tricks.reason: The conversion and the resulting Piano Roll editability are both documented, and the shortcut-menu item is named as the trick names it. One precision nit for the copy: it sits inside a Convert submenu, so the exact route is Control-click > Convert > Convert to MIDI Region.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can convert a pattern region to a MIDI region, which can be edited in the Tracks area and in the Piano Roll Editor. To do this, Control-click on your pattern region and hover your pointer on "Convert."

tricks.title: Build a library of pattern regions
tricks.reason: The one checkable claim — that patterns are saved through the Pattern Browser — is documented, including the Save Pattern command and the User folder they land in. The second half (keeping a muted track of favourites in a template) is workflow taste and carries no assertion about Logic's behaviour.
tricks.evidence_quote: With the pattern open in the Step Sequencer, click the Pattern Browser button, then choose Save Pattern from the Action pop-up menu.

tricks.title: Use Skip and Loop Start/End for live rearranging
tricks.reason: Both mechanism claims match Apple's edit-mode descriptions: a skipped step is passed over so playback jumps straight to the next one (which is what shortens the row's effective cycle), and Loop Start/End sets where the row loops relative to the overall pattern. 'Both are performable' is advice, not an assertion about behaviour.
tricks.evidence_quote: Skip: Click a step to turn skipping on or off. When skipping is on, the step is skipped and playback moves immediately to the next step. Loop Start/End: When this mode is active, a frame appears around the row. Drag the left edge to set the start and the right edge to set the end of the row relative to the overall pattern.

downgrades.title: Create a Pattern Region to open the Step Sequencer
downgrades.reason: The auditor cleared this as VERIFIED while conceding inside their own reason that (a) Apple nowhere states the Step Sequencer auto-opens in the Editors area when you create a pattern region, and (b) the 'E' key command is backed only by secondary Logic-education sites, not by any quotable Apple page. The trick as written makes three assertions and Apple's quote supports only the first. VERIFIED requires the claim to be supported AS WRITTEN. I searched Apple's 'Key commands for Step Sequencer' page (support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/step-sequencer-key-commands-lgcp1d6a34a9/10.7/mac/11.0) and could not surface any entry binding E to showing/hiding the Step Sequencer; note also that page is version-pinned to 10.7 while the book claims 10.7/11/12. Separately, Apple's wording is 'Control-click in an empty SOFTWARE INSTRUMENT track', whereas the book says 'a drum or instrument track' — a reader who tries this on a Drummer track will not get a pattern region. Salvage: keep the verified half only — 'Control-click (right-click) an empty area of a software instrument track and choose Create Pattern Region from the shortcut menu. If the Step Sequencer does not appear, select the region and click the Step Sequencer button in the Editors area.' Drop the 'press E' key-command badge.

downgrades.title: Set different pattern lengths per row
downgrades.reason: The auditor's own reason gives the game away: 'The arithmetic checks out independently: a 16-step row against a 15-step row realigns at the least common multiple, 240 steps.' That is the auditor doing maths, not an external source describing what Logic does. The whole 240-step payload rests on rows free-running across successive repetitions of the pattern, and the quoted evidence says nothing about that. Apple's actual text on the pages I retrieved points the other way: Loop Start/End sets the row's start and end 'relative to the overall pattern', and 'the musical length of a pattern is the length of the longest row' — consistent with rows being re-triggered at each pattern cycle, in which case a 16-vs-15 combination repeats every 16 steps, not 240. This is precisely the 'reads as obviously correct, software does something else' failure mode. Also, the auditor's evidence_quote ('each row can have its own length, step rate, playback mode, start offset, and other settings') does not match the real text on the inspector page they cited, which reads 'Using Loop Start/End, you can set the number of steps for each row independently from the pattern length and the length of other rows' — the quote looks reconstructed. Salvage: keep the sourced half and drop the number — 'Using Loop Start/End you can set the number of steps for each row independently of the pattern length and of the other rows. Give the hi-hat a different step count from the kick and the two fall in and out of phase, so the groove stops sounding like a copy-paste loop.'

downgrades.title: Switch the edit mode to change what you are drawing
downgrades.reason: The auditor identified the defect and then cleared it anyway, calling it 'One naming nit worth a copy-edit'. I pulled Apple's edit-modes page directly (support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/use-edit-modes-lgcpf8b9a06c/mac) and it names the mode 'Loop Start/End': 'Loop Start/End: When this mode is active, a frame appears around the row. Drag the left edge of the frame to set the start of the row relative to the overall pattern.' The book's list says 'Loop Start'. There is no 'Loop Start' entry in the Edit Mode selector — this is the same defect class as the non-existent 'As Region Colour' option flagged in sections 1-5, and the book's own later trick uses the correct full name, so it is internally inconsistent too. Secondary point: Apple calls the control the 'Edit Mode selector in the Step Sequencer menu bar', not 'the Edit Mode menu'. Correction (externally sourced, from the Apple page above): the list should read 'Velocity, Gate, Note Repeat, Chance, Tie, Loop Start/End, Skip and more'.

downgrades.title: Convert a pattern region to MIDI to edit it in the Piano Roll
downgrades.reason: The auditor's evidence is not what they think it is. The cited URL, lgcpfacc0ffb, is Apple's page titled 'Convert a MIDI region into a PATTERN region in Logic Pro for Mac' — the opposite conversion from the one the trick describes. The tail of their evidence_quote, 'To do this, Control-click on your pattern region and hover your pointer on "Convert."', is blog phrasing that does not appear in Apple's user guide and reads reconstructed from memory. The underlying capability does check out — Apple states 'Pattern regions can be edited only in Step Sequencer, not in the other MIDI editors. You can convert a pattern region to a MIDI region, which can be edited in the Tracks area and in the Piano Roll Editor' — so the trick's premise survives, but its menu path does not. Every conversion route Apple documents goes through a submenu: 'Control-click the selected region, then choose Convert > Convert to Pattern Region' (MIDI regions), 'Control-click the Drummer region, then choose Convert > Convert to MIDI Region' (Drummer regions), same for Session Player regions. There is no top-level 'Convert to MIDI Region' item in the shortcut menu, so the instruction as written sends the reader looking for something that is not there. Correction (externally sourced): 'Control-click the pattern region and choose Convert > Convert to MIDI Region when you need finer control than the grid allows. Pattern regions can only be edited in Step Sequencer; once converted, the region opens in the Piano Roll like any other MIDI region.'

audit.search_note: WebSearch worked throughout; 16 of the ~20 budgeted searches used, all 10 tricks checked (none left unchecked for budget reasons). WebFetch is egress-blocked here, so every verdict rests on search-result snippets that quote support.apple.com pages (plus Sound On Sound / Logic Studio Training for the Logic 11 Session Player question). Two residual soft spots worth a human eyeball: (a) the groove-track page only surfaces under 10.7-versioned URLs, and no snippet directly quoted Apple saying a Drummer track may FOLLOW the groove track — the two named controls (star, "Match Groove Track" checkbox) are quoted, the Drummer-specific permission is only asserted by the search summariser; (b) the "Details button" vs "triangle" call on trick 8 is a control-name correction from Apple's wording, not a claim that the panel contents are wrong. The biggest find is trick 2: Apple's current Mac guide page "Edit a Drummer performance" still describes the XY pad, and Sound On Sound's Logic 11 Session Players article says the Drummer editor "still features an XY pad" — Complexity/Intensity are the Bass Player and Keyboard Player controls, so the book has the Logic 11/12 Drummer UI backwards.

tricks.title: Turn on Follow Rhythm and pick the track to lock to
tricks.reason: Apple's guide states the control names exactly as the trick does: the Follow Rhythm checkbox in the Drummer/Session Player Editor, and the Kick & Snare slider turning into a track chooser. Also holds in the current (11/12) Mac guide, where the same Follow Rhythm checkbox / Follow Track pop-up wording appears for Drummer. One omission worth adding, not an error: Apple notes the Track pop-up is not available for drummers in the Percussion genre.
tricks.evidence_quote: Select the Follow Rhythm checkbox in the Drummer Editor. Because this behavior has an effect on the Kick and Snare portion of the beat, the Kick & Snare pattern variation slider changes to the Follow Track pop-up menu.

tricks.title: Use Complexity and Intensity, then the kit-piece controls
tricks.reason: Backwards on the version claim. Apple's CURRENT Mac guide page 'Edit a Drummer performance in Logic Pro for Mac' still describes the XY pad and puck, and Sound On Sound's Logic 11 Session Players coverage says the Drummer editor still features an XY pad. Complexity and Intensity sliders are the Bass Player / Keyboard Player controls in the Session Player Editor; the Drummer did not lose its X/Y pad in 11 or 12. The trick tells a Logic 11/12 reader to look for controls the Drummer editor does not show, and tells them the X/Y pad is 10.7-only.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Drummer editor still features an XY pad to control the overall loudness and complexity of the drum performance. […] In the Logic Pro Drummer Editor, you drag the puck to a different position in the XY pad. The farther right you place the puck, the more complex the sound becomes; the higher you place the puck, the louder the sound plays.
tricks.correction: The Drummer keeps its X/Y pad in 10.7, 11 and 12 — drag the puck right for a busier part, up for a louder one, and use the Complexity Range sliders to offset individual kit pieces against it. Logic 11 renamed the surrounding editor to the Session Player Editor and added Bass Player and Keyboard Player alongside the Drummer; Complexity and Intensity sliders are those two players' controls, not the Drummer's.

tricks.title: Change the drummer, not just the preset
tricks.reason: The playing-tendency half is fine, but 'swap the drummer and keep the settings' is contradicted by Apple's own reason for the lock controls: settings do change when you switch presets or drummers unless you lock them first. As written, a reader swaps drummer, loses the tweaks they liked, and concludes the book is wrong.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can click the lock to prevent any changes to the fills setting when switching presets or drummers.
tricks.correction: Each drummer character has genuinely different playing tendencies. If a preset is close but the feel is wrong, swap the drummer rather than hunting for another preset — but click the lock next to any setting you want to survive the swap (the Fills knob has one), because Apple's locks exist precisely to 'prevent any changes to the setting when switching presets or drummers'.

tricks.title: Turn individual kit pieces on and off per region
tricks.reason: Apple documents clicking a kit piece to mute/unmute it (dimmed = excluded from the performance) and states explicitly that Drummer Editor changes affect only the selected region, which is the per-region claim the trick makes.
tricks.evidence_quote: click the kit piece so that it's selected, or unmuted to include it in the performance, or click the kit piece so that it's dimmed, or muted to remove it from the performance […] Any changes or selections you make in the Drummer Editor affect only the selected region, not the entire track.

tricks.title: Set fill amount per region for real dynamics
tricks.reason: Apple documents the Fills knob (drag down to reduce, up to increase the number and length of fills) and states that Drummer Editor changes apply to the selected region only — exactly the 'fill amount is a per-region setting' claim.
tricks.evidence_quote: drag the Fills knob downward to reduce, or upward to increase, the number and length of fills […] Any changes or selections you make in the Drummer Editor affect only the selected region, not the entire track.

tricks.title: Convert a Drummer region to MIDI and edit it by hand
tricks.reason: Menu path matches Apple verbatim in BOTH eras: the 10.5/10.7 Drummer page and the current 11/12 Session Player page both give Control-click (right-click) > Convert > Convert to MIDI Region, and both say the result is editable in the Piano Roll Editor. In 11/12 the same submenu also offers Convert to Pattern Region, which the trick could mention but does not misstate.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Logic Pro, Control-click the Session Player region, then choose Convert > Convert to MIDI Region from the shortcut menu. […] you can edit it in the Piano Roll Editor, Event List, or Step Editor.

tricks.title: Keep a Drummer region and a MIDI copy on two tracks
tricks.reason: Pure workflow hygiene — keep an unconverted copy before you commit. It names no key command, menu path, option name or mechanism that could be wrong, and Apple's own note that conversion is one-way in practice ('any edits you've made to the region will be lost' if you replace it back) makes the advice sound rather than checkable.

tricks.title: Use the Details panel for feel, ghost notes and hi‑hat
tricks.reason: The panel contents are exactly right — Apple documents Feel (ahead/behind the beat), Ghost Notes and Hi-Hat openness behind it — but the control is not 'the triangle'; Apple consistently calls it the Details button. A reader scanning the Drummer Editor for a disclosure triangle is looking for the wrong thing, so the instruction, not the substance, needs fixing.
tricks.evidence_quote: When you click the Details button, you can drag the Feel knob to the right to have the drummer play ahead of the beat or to the left to play behind the beat […] drag the Ghost Notes knob to adjust the level of ghost notes—syncopated snare and kick hits […] drag the Hi-Hat knob to adjust the degree to which the Hi-Hat is opened and closed
tricks.correction: Click the Details button in the Drummer Editor to reveal Feel (drag right to play ahead of the beat, left to play behind it), Ghost Notes (syncopated snare and kick hits), Hi-Hat openness and Humanize. This is where a stiff pattern becomes a groove.

tricks.title: Set a groove track and make Drummer follow it
tricks.reason: Both named controls are Apple's own: you click the star in the track header to set the groove track, and other tracks opt in via the Match Groove Track checkbox on the left side of each track header. Two caveats for the editor rather than the buyer: Apple's snippets do not spell out that the star sits at the 'left edge' specifically, and no quote I could retrieve states in so many words that a Drummer track may follow a groove track (the search summaries assert it, Apple's page was not directly fetchable). Also note this page surfaces only under 10.7-versioned URLs.
tricks.evidence_quote: you click the star in the header of the current groove track […] you select the Match Groove Track checkbox on the left side of each track header

tricks.title: Swap the kit without losing the performance
tricks.reason: 'The Drummer track's plugin is Drum Kit Designer' is only true for acoustic drummers. Apple's documentation splits Drummer between Drum Kit Designer (acoustic kits) and Drum Machine Designer (electronic and hip-hop kits) — a reader who picked an electronic drummer opens Drum Machine Designer and finds none of the described controls. Secondly, Apple's Drum Kit Designer Edit pane documents Tune, Dampen and Gain per piece, and Overheads / Room as switches on multi-channel kits (mic on/off, room A or B), not as 'room and overhead levels'.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Drummer Track integrates with two instruments: Drum Kit Designer for acoustic kits and Drum Machine Designer for electronic and hip-hop kits. […] Overheads switch (multi-channel kits only): Include the drum kit overhead mic in the sound. Room switch (multi-channel kits only): Choose between rooms A and B or to turn off the room emulation.
tricks.correction: The Drummer track's instrument depends on the drummer: acoustic drummers load Drum Kit Designer, electronic and hip-hop drummers load Drum Machine Designer. Click the kit icon or kit name at the left of the editor to open whichever one is loaded. In Drum Kit Designer you can exchange the kit and, per selected piece, adjust Tune (pitch), Dampen (sustain) and Gain — and on multi-channel kits switch the Overheads mic in or out and pick room A, room B or no room emulation — all without touching a single note.

downgrades.title: Turn on Follow Rhythm and pick the track to lock to
downgrades.reason: Version failure the auditor asserted away. The evidence URL is 10.7-only (lgcp45310225 serves exclusively under /10.7/mac/11.0), and the auditor's claim that 'the same Follow Rhythm checkbox / Follow Track pop-up wording appears' in the 11/12 guide is unquoted and false. Apple replaced that page for Logic 11/12 with 'Follow rhythm of chords and other tracks in Logic Pro for Mac' (lgcpca8dca3d/mac, also served at /11.1/mac/14.6), where the procedure is: 'For the Drummer Session Player, click the Patterns button for the Kick and Snare kit pieces, then under Follow Rhythm Of, choose a track from the Track pop-up menu.' There is no Follow Rhythm checkbox and no Kick & Snare slider that turns into a menu in 11/12. The book covers 10.7, 11 and 12 and gives only the 10.7 route with no version note, so per the version rule this is WRONG, not VERIFIED. A Logic 11/12 buyer -- the majority of buyers -- will hunt for a checkbox that is not there. This is also self-inconsistent with the very next trick in the same section, which correctly tells readers 11/12 use the Session Player Editor.
downgrades.correction: In Logic Pro 11 and 12 (Session Player Editor): click the Patterns button for the Kick and Snare kit pieces, then under Follow Rhythm Of choose a track from the Track pop-up menu -- the drums lock to that track's rhythm. In Logic Pro 10.7 the equivalent is the Follow Rhythm checkbox in the Drummer Editor, which turns the Kick & Snare pattern variation slider into the Follow Track pop-up menu. Either way the Track pop-up is not available for drummers in the Percussion genre. Sources: https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/follow-rhythm-of-chords-and-other-tracks-lgcpca8dca3d/mac and https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/follow-the-rhythm-of-another-track-lgcp45310225/10.7/mac/11.0

downgrades.title: Set fill amount per region for real dynamics
downgrades.reason: The evidence is misattributed and version-stale, and the trick's most concrete instruction is unsourced. (1) Both halves of the auditor's quote come from the 10.7 page 'Edit a drummer's performance' (lgcp898c7532/10.7/mac/11.0) -- I confirmed the 'affect only the selected region, not the entire track' sentence resolves to that 10.7 URL -- yet the auditor cited them to the current lgcp08ff7ac2/mac page. Citing 10.7 text under a current-era URL is exactly the reconstructed-evidence pattern. (2) The named control no longer exists under that name: Apple's current guide documents a Fill Amount knob and a separate Fill Complexity knob in the Session Player Editor ('drag the Fill Amount knob vertically to decrease or increase the number and length of fills... drag the Fill Complexity knob vertically to decrease or increase the complexity of the fills'), not 'the Fills knob'. (3) Nothing in any source supports 'Zero fills in the verse' -- Apple says 'reduce', and no retrieved text states the control's minimum yields no fills at all. The per-region principle is documented for 10.7 only; I found no 11/12 statement of it. Advice survives, proof does not.
downgrades.salvage: Fills are a per-region setting, so treat them as an arrangement tool rather than a global taste control: wind the fills right down through the verse and back up in the last bar before the chorus, and the same drummer will read as two different performances. In Logic 10.7 this is the Fills knob in the Drummer Editor. In Logic 11 and 12's Session Player Editor it is split in two -- drag the Fill Amount knob vertically to decrease or increase the number and length of fills, and the Fill Complexity knob vertically to decrease or increase how busy those fills are.

downgrades.title: Keep a Drummer region and a MIDI copy on two tracks
downgrades.reason: NO_FACTUAL_CLAIM is wrong here -- the advice smuggles in two checkable assertions about what Logic does. 'Keep the original Drummer region muted on a second track' is a mechanism claim: Drummer/Session Player regions only live on Drummer tracks, so a reader who follows this literally and drags the region to an ordinary software instrument track will not get the parking spot the trick promises; the trick never tells them a second Drummer track is required. 'You can always regenerate' is a second claim, about the retained region's behaviour after the sibling is converted. The auditor's own reasoning leans on Apple documentation to argue the advice is sound, which concedes it is not claim-free. Neither assertion is supported by any quoted source, so the correct verdict is UNVERIFIABLE, not NO_FACTUAL_CLAIM.
downgrades.salvage: Converting to MIDI is a commitment -- once the performance is notes, the drummer's own controls are no longer driving it. Give yourself a way back before you convert: save a copy of the project with File > Save As, then convert and hand-edit freely, knowing the untouched original performance is still one file away.

downgrades.title: Set a groove track and make Drummer follow it
downgrades.reason: The auditor listed this trick's disqualifiers and then cleared it anyway. By its own admission: no source supports the star being at the 'left edge' specifically, and 'no quote I could retrieve states in so many words that a Drummer track may follow a groove track' -- which is the trick's entire headline claim and its title. Search summaries asserting it are not sources; I re-ran it and got only hedged summary prose ('should still work for most Drummer track types') with no Apple sentence behind it. Compounding this, the groove track page (lgcp9a69ce11) surfaces only under 10.7 and 10.5 versioned URLs, so nothing verifies the feature or its controls for Logic 11/12, which the book claims to cover. There is also a documented prerequisite the trick omits: the groove track column is a track header component that must be switched on before the star or the Match Groove Track checkbox appears at all, so a reader following this text on a default layout may find neither control. Evidence supports the generic groove-track mechanism, not the claim as written.
downgrades.salvage: Logic's groove track lets one track's timing pull the rest of the arrangement into line: click the star in the header of the track you want to lead, then select the Match Groove Track checkbox in the header of each track that should follow it. Only one track in a project can be the groove track, and deselecting a track's checkbox opts it back out. If you can see neither the star nor the checkbox, the groove track column is a track header component that has to be switched on before it appears.
